raw_case_text:
In brief, the 29-year old student presented to her general practitioner with recurrent fever up to 40 C in December 2019. Medically, she and her relatives had an uneventful past. After fever persistence for more than two weeks she was admitted to hospital for an extensive work-up. In clinical and ultrasound examinations, abdominal lymph node enlargements and a marked hepatosplenomegaly were noticed. These findings were confirmed in positron emission computer tomography (PET-CT) scanning ( Figures 1A, B ). Her blood counts showed pancytopenia (WBC 1.5 x 109/l, neutrophils 1.0 x 109/l, lymphocytes 0.35 x 109/l, monocytes 0.01 x 109/l, hemoglobin 76 g/l, platelets 78 x 109/l), and additional lab testing revealed hyperferritinemia (3860 g/l), hypertriglyceridemia (4.56 mmol/l), increased serum levels of aspartate aminotransferase (AST 79 U/l), soluble interleukin-2 receptor (sIL-2R, 2710 U/l), and lactate dehydrogenase (LDH 626 U/L). Although fibrinogen was normal (5.1 g/l), a diagnosis of HLH was made based on HLH-2004 criteria [7/8 fulfilled including impaired NK-cell function, see below; ] and an HScore of 239 points [98-99% probability of hemophagocytosis; ], respectively.
After ruling out Leishmania spp., HIV, EBV, and CMV infections by serology and PCR (peripheral blood and bone marrow, BM), biopsies of retroperitoneal lymph nodes were taken. Surprisingly, histopathology did not show lymphoma but demonstrated granulomatous lymphadenitis including acid-fast bacteria, which were further classified as Mycobacterium avium by genotyping (MycoDirect 1.7 LCD array, Chipron, Germany). M. avium was also detected in BM and cultured from bronchoalveolar lavage samples, giving the diagnosis of NTM infection triggering HLH. In BM cytology and histopathology no signs of myelodysplasia were identified.
Treatment with amikacin, azithromycin, ethambutol and rifampicin was initiated promptly, however, the fever and other HLH-signs persisted. Only after intensive immunosuppressive therapy including high-dose dexamethasone, ciclosporin A, intravenous immunoglobulins, and repetitive courses of etoposide (75 mg/m2, twice weekly) the HLH-related symptoms could temporarily be ameliorated. The cause for HLH and NTM was further investigated including CTL and NK-cell function analysis in CD107a-assays. These indicated significant degranulation impairments in both effector cell types ( Figure 2 ). Perforin expression was normal, and genetic variants in UNC13D, STXBP2, RAB27A, and STX11 were excluded in Sanger sequencing. Subsequently, next generation sequencing (NovaSeq 6000 NGS platform) of genes associated with NTM infections [CYBB, GATA2, IFNGR1/R2, IL12B, IL12RB1/RB2, IL23R, IRF8, ISG15, JAK1, RORC, SPPL2A, STAT1, TYK2; ; ] was performed. As result, a novel GATA2 variant (c.177C>G, p.Tyr59Ter) in heterozygous form was identified (DNA from peripheral blood and mucosa cells).
Considering disseminated NTM infection and secondary HLH resulting from primary immunodeficiency due to germline GATA2 deficiency, we aimed for alloHSCT as curative therapy. An HLA-matched unrelated donor (MUD 10/10) was identified, and the patient underwent alloHSCT following reduced-intensity conditioning with fludarabine (150 mg/m2) and treosulfan (30 g/m2) in September 2020. Graft-versus-Host disease (GvHD) prophylaxis consisted of post-transplant cyclophosphamide (100 mg/kg), mycophenolate-mofetil, and ciclosporin. Prior to alloHSCT, the antimycobacterial treatment was switched to azithromycin, clofazimine, and ethambutol. The fever and HLH-signs completely resolved after full hematopoietic engraftment. In the absence of GvHD, ciclosporin was ceased at day +98 post-alloHSCT. Following diagnosis of moderate hepatotoxicity, which appeared drug-related in a liver biopsy, all antibiotics were stopped 6 months after alloHSCT and 1 year after disease onset, respectively. PET-CT scanning at that time demonstrated complete remission of all inflammatory manifestations ( Figures 1C, D ).

subjective.chief_complaint: A 29-year-old female student presented in December 2019 with a >2-week history of recurrent high fevers up to 40 C.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Previously healthy, the patient presented to her general practitioner in December 2019 with recurrent fevers peaking at 40 C that persisted for more than 2 weeks, prompting hospital admission where marked hepatosplenomegaly, abdominal lymphadenopathy, and pancytopenia were identified.
subjective.past_medical_history: Previously healthy 29-year-old student with an unremarkable personal and family medical history.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for persistent high fevers up to 40 C.

objective.physical_examination: Febrile (up to 40 C) with marked hepatosplenomegaly.
objective.routine_investigations: Labs showed pancytopenia (WBC 1.5 x 10^9/L, neutrophils 1.0 x 10^9/L, lymphocytes 0.35 x 10^9/L, monocytes 0.01 x 10^9/L, Hb 76 g/L, platelets 78 x 10^9/L), ferritin 3,860 ug/L, triglycerides 4.56 mmol/L, AST 79 U/L, LDH 626 U/L, and normal fibrinogen (5.1 g/L). Serologies and peripheral blood/bone marrow PCRs for Leishmania spp., HIV, EBV, and CMV were negative. Abdominal ultrasound showed abdominal lymphadenopathy and marked hepatosplenomegaly.
objective.advanced_workup: Soluble IL-2 receptor (sIL-2R) was 2,710 U/L, HScore was 239 (98-99% HLH probability; 7/8 HLH-2004 criteria met), and CD107a assays showed impaired CTL and NK-cell degranulation with normal perforin expression. PET-CT confirmed marked hepatosplenomegaly and hypermetabolic abdominal lymphadenopathy. Retroperitoneal lymph node biopsy revealed granulomatous lymphadenitis with acid-fast bacilli genotyped as Mycobacterium avium (also detected in bone marrow and cultured from BAL fluid), while targeted NGS (NovaSeq 6000) of blood and mucosal DNA identified a novel heterozygous germline nonsense variant in GATA2 (c.177C>G, p.Tyr59Ter).

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Lymphoma and viral/parasitic triggers (including Leishmania spp., EBV, CMV, and HIV) were excluded; retroperitoneal lymph node biopsy, bone marrow detection, BAL culture, and targeted NGS confirmed disseminated Mycobacterium avium infection triggering secondary hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH) as the first manifestation of germline GATA2 deficiency (c.177C>G, p.Tyr59Ter). Following antimycobacterial therapy (amikacin, azithromycin, ethambutol, and rifampicin, later transitioned to azithromycin, clofazimine, and ethambutol) and HLH immunochemotherapy (high-dose dexamethasone, cyclosporine A, IVIG, and twice-weekly etoposide 75 mg/m2), curative 10/10 matched unrelated donor allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (fludarabine/treosulfan conditioning) in September 2020 achieved complete hematologic and PET-CT remission at 1 year.
